piezas.titulo: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense
piezas.resumenOriginal: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense STAR Admin Fri, 02/17/2023 - 20:50 Join STAR Institute and some of its expert clinicians for three nights of learning as we explore the keys to a sensory-informed life. Each night, STAR's Clinical Director will be joined by a different STAR therapist to share tips and strategies around some of families' most often asked questions including: “How can I support and be there for my family when I am constantly feeling burned out?” “What can I do to help my child transition from thing to thing/place to place more smoothly?" “We feel like we walk on egg shells around our child. Why is that and what can we do?" Each night will begin with a 30-40 minute conversation led by the therapist before a live Q&A where you can ask STAR’s occupational therapists and mental health providers your own questions. Discussions You Don't Want to Miss: Caring for Yourself So You Can Care for Others Keys to Successful Transitions in Life’s Big and Small Moments Beyond Fight, Flight, or Freeze: How to Support Regulation STAR Voices You'll Hear From: Mim Ochsenbein, MSW, OTR/L (she/her) Clinical Director Mim Ochsenbein, MSW, OTR/L has been a practicing pediatric occupational therapist for over 25 years. She received her BSc in Occupational Therapy from the University of Southern California (USC) in 1996 and her MSW from the University of California-Los Angeles (UCLA) in 2012. She has received advanced training in sensory integration (SIPT certification, STAR ProCert1, STAR ProCert2), listening therapy (Therapeutic Listening, iLs), feeding therapy (SOS), DIR, mental health (DC:0-5 Diagnostic Classification of Mental Health Disorders of Infancy and Early Childhood), and infant massage (CIMI). Her work in occupational therapy with children and youth has occurred in a variety of settings including early intervention, school based, clinic based, mental health and private practice. As a social worker, she provided case management, program development, and program management. Mim has taught both university level (California State-Dominguez Hills) and professional continuing education courses since 2013, spoken internationally, and has co-authored works for professional publications. She has been in her current role at STAR Institute since 2017 at the invitation of Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, PhD, FAOTA, OTR. Gina Crites, OTR/L, MFTC Counselor Gina has a Master’s degree in Marriage and Family Therapy from the University of New Hampshire (2009). She currently provides therapy to individuals (8 years through adulthood), couples, and families in-person or through telehealth (Colorado residents only). Clients would describe Gina’s style as reflective, collaborative, and experiential. She has a calm yet dynamic presence and works from a compassionate, curious, and empowering stance. Gina’s practice is rooted in attachment and systems theories, making her truly a relationally focused therapist. As such, she believes that our greatest healing occurs in the context of relationships. She has always been oriented toward a biopsychosocial approach to her theory of change, thereby honoring the importance of the mind-body connection. She believes that within a safe space and through our attuned relationship with Self and others, we all have the power to tune into our instinct towards healing. With her early career in occupational therapy, Gina has incredible understanding of the importance of self-determination for clients: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. This—coupled with her deep understanding of sensory integration and processing and the importance of occupational roles—truly sets her apart. Her practice honors and respects each person’s unique history and individual differences, and sets clients up for experiencing a deeper sense of self and relational health, on the clients’ own terms. Gina was drawn to couples and family therapy for its non-pathologizing approach to viewing clients’ problems. While biological factors certainly play a role, so do clients’ experiences within their families, partnerships, and larger society. She is passionate about empowering parents to reflect on and integrate their own experiences in service of their children’s health and wellness, as well as their own. “Society does not prioritize proactively supporting its members’ health and therefore, parents and families are not set up for success. This is particularly true for oppressed groups, the poorly included and the disenfranchised.” She believes that parents innately know how high the stakes are and are doing their best, and, like all of us, only benefit from being and feeling less alone in their pain and struggle. Gina is especially equipped to support neurodivergent individuals, couples and families, as well as those navigating issues around disability and chronic illness. She is capable of easily moving between deep therapeutic work, parent coaching and individual skills training - making her a versatile therapist. She has experience supporting clients with life transitions, anxiety, depression, non-suicidal self-harm, suicidal ideation, recovery from adverse childhood experiences and trauma, developing deeper emotional awareness, identifying and leaving behind maladaptive coping patterns, and improving self-esteem. Above all, Gina is a sensory informed, neurodiversity affirming and LGBTQIA+ allied, culturally sensitive and attachment-focused therapist with a special interest in interpersonal neurobiology who strongly believes in the healing power of making sense of our experiences in the context of relationships where we feel seen, heard, and understood. Jayna Niblock, PhD, OTD, OTR/L, BCP Occupational Therapist Jayna graduated from Simpson College with a bachelor's degree in biology and Spanish. She then completed a doctorate in occupational therapy at Creighton University. Jayna was the first Occupational Therapy Pediatric Resident (now called Fellowship) with Creighton University following her occupational therapy degree. During this time, she received advanced training in Sensory Integration and Processing, feeding, the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, and education. Jayna has worked in a variety of pediatric settings prior to coming to STAR Institute and is Board Certified in Pediatrics through the American Occupational Therapy Association (AOTA). She currently serves as the Technology Coordinator for the Sensory Integration and Processing Special Interest Section for the AOTA. Jayna enjoys engaging in play-based therapy focused on relationship building between a child and their family. She brings a strengths-based approach to support the child and family achieve their goals in life. Jayna has advanced training in Sensory Integration and Processing differences including Mentorship Certification through the STAR Institute. She is also trained in Integrated Listening Systems (iLS) and the Sequential Oral Sensory (SOS) approach to feeding. Jayna has a Doctor of Philosophy in Educational Leadership and seeks to support practice through research and evidence. Jayna is an ally to the neurodiverse community and strives to learn more and integrate practices which support neurodiverse persons to build a strong sense of self and live their most sensory-rich lives. Chelsea Marquette, (COTA/L) Licensed Certified Occupational Therapy Assistant Chelsea graduated with her Bachelor of Science in Family Studies and Human Services from Kansas State University in 2014 and then in 2018 graduated from Pueblo Community College with an Associate of Applied Science Occupational Therapy Assistant. Since 2018 she has worked in multidisciplinary team pediatric outpatient settings and post-acute care rehab with adults. She has supervised four OTA students and in May 2022 presented for OTAC on social emotional development in children and teens with her past supervising OTR. Chelsea enjoys building relationships with families and helping them find joy together. Her special interests include providing trauma-informed and neurodiverse-affirming care. She has taken courses to expand her understanding of trauma through the Starr Commonwealth and with Bessel van der Kolk. She has also taken the Learn Play Thrive Approach to Autism course. She is a member of AOTA and enjoys learning more to become a better OTA. During her free time, Chelsea likes soaking up the sunshine, reading, yoga, and going to museums. piezas.titulo: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
piezas.resumenOriginal: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini! In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub , she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong ” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.” Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto , an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable. The AI Arms Race On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making. These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi , IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through. Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics. Burden on Academics Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop. Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake Paper Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini Ghost citations Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated. Questionable scientific claims An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable. Too many acronyms The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract. Round 2: The AI-Research Paper Created by the autonomous research system FARS Too many preprints The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints. Nonsense in a figure One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.” AI artifacts Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots. There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record. Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky , cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles. Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.” Blurred Lines My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System) , AutoResearchClaw , The AIScientist-v2 , Zochi , AI Researcher , and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw , for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery. The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.” FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours , was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma . “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su , Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.) Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test. Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously. Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours. At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney. Round 2: Attempt to Publish Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one. “Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem. In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated. Automation Changing the Landscape Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process. “FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge ,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.” In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?” A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future? Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.” In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?” To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’” Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent. piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Altered interhemispheric functional cooperation in persistent postural-perceptual dizziness
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundPersistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) is associated with altered multisensory processing, but its hemispheric functional organization remains poorly understood. We investigated hemispheric functional lateralization and interhemispheric cooperation in PPPD and explored their associations with clinical symptoms and neurotransmitter density maps.MethodsA total of 47 patients with PPPD and 52 healthy controls (HCs) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Whole-brain maps of the autonomy index (AI) and connectivity between functionally homotopic voxels (CFH) were generated. Between-group differences were assessed using permutation-based analyses adjusted for age, sex, and mean framewise displacement (FD). Associations with clinical measures and spatial correspondence with 13 neurotransmitter density maps were also examined.ResultsThe PPPD and HC groups did not differ significantly in age, sex, or educational level (all p > 0.05). Patients with PPPD had lower MoCA-BJ scores and higher HAMA-14, HAMD-24, PSQI, and DHI scores than HCs, whereas MMSE scores did not differ significantly. No between-group differences in AI survived family-wise error (FWE) correction. By contrast, in the primary analysis, patients with PPPD showed significantly reduced CFH in the right calcarine cortex, right cuneus, left inferior and middle occipital gyri, left inferior parietal lobule, and right middle temporal gyrus. However, no CFH clusters survived cluster-level FWE correction after separately adjusting for HAMA-14, HAMD-24, or PSQI scores. After adjustment for age, sex, and mean FD, CFH in the right calcarine cortex and left inferior parietal lobule showed negative associations with DHI total and DHI-E scores, respectively (Shepherd’s π = −0.363 and −0.452), but neither association remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. The CFH group-difference map showed nominal positive spatial correlations with the D2R and VAChT density maps, but these associations were not significant after FDR correction.ConclusionIn primary analysis, PPPD patients exhibited reduced interhemispheric functional cooperation in visual, visuospatial and multisensory regions, while no AI differences survived FWE correction. However, these CFH findings were sensitive to adjustment for affective symptoms and sleep quality; the relative contributions of PPPD, affective symptoms and sleep disturbance remain uncertain. Clinical and neurotransmitter density-map associations did not survive FDR correction and are exploratory.

piezas.titulo: Epidermal Langerhans Cells Act as Neuroimmune Regulators of Pain and Itch
piezas.resumenOriginal: Neuroimmune interactions in the skin coordinate immune defense and somatosensory perception, yet how immune cells shape sensory signaling remains poorly defined. Here, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), epidermal antigen-presenting cells, function as local immune-derived amplifiers of cutaneous sensory signaling. Anatomical and transcriptomic analyses reveal preferential LC association with non-peptidergic sensory neurons. LC activation increases neuronal and behavioral responses to thermal, mechanical, and pruritic stimuli without directly exciting sensory neurons, whereas LC inhibition or ablation selectively reduces pruritogen-evoked itch. We identified semaphorin 7A as a candidate LC-expressed mediator. Semaphorin 7A sensitized cultured sensory neurons to chloroquine and histamine, and neutralizing semaphorin 7A abolished the increase in chloroquine-evoked scratching produced by LC activation. Its receptor PlexinC1 was expressed by most MrgprA3 pruriceptors and blocking PlexinC1 reduced semaphorin 7A-evoked neuronal responses. Together, these findings identify epidermal LCs as local immune-derived amplifiers that regulate the responsiveness of cutaneous sensory circuits and identify semaphorin 7A as a mediator of LC-induced itch potentiation.

piezas.titulo: Resolving the apparent paradox of multisensory expertise: coupling priors, common-cause priors, and how to distinguish among them
piezas.resumenOriginal: Perceptual expertise is widely assumed to refine multisensory perception, yet the empirical literature appears inconsistent. Trained musicians show narrower audiovisual temporal integration windows and quicker segregation, whereas experienced wine tasters seem more influenced by a wine's color in their aroma and flavor judgments than novices are. We argue that the inconsistency arises from a conflation of two formally distinct quantities: the prior probability that concurrent signals arise from a common source, and the coupling between the values of signals that share one. We present a generative model in which both are free parameters, along with channel precision and a decision criterion, that contains causal-inference and coupling-prior models as special cases. The model shows that the correlation between the values of two signals across an environment reflects only the product of the two priors, so that a correlation-tracking learner acquires the coupling when the signals always share a source, whereas separating the two priors requires representing causal structure; that binary common-source reports confound the common-cause prior with the decision criterion; that the coupling trades off against the measurement noise of the influencing channel unless its precision is measured independently; and that the two priors leave distinct signatures in how cross-modal influence varies with disparity. When the source is fixed, as for the color and odor of a wine, tighter coupling alone produces the conjunction of greater displacement by color and better discrimination between wines reported for experienced tasters, which no change in odor precision can produce. Simulations of a test battery combining continuous estimates, common-source reports and discrimination thresholds show that the parameters can be recovered, that a within-subject dissociation can be detected with conventional sample sizes under illustrative effect sizes, and that recovery fails in certain cases. The account yields a rule classifying environments by their base rate of common causation and their coupling strength, and the same ambiguity attends claims about altered multisensory processing in autism and aging. We also show that the most cited demonstration of expert susceptibility to color contains no expertise manipulation, and suggest that apparent expert biases may reflectwind calibration to real-world statistics.

piezas.titulo: Chronic environmental cold stress increases migraine susceptibility associated with regional dysregulation of RBFOX1 and PTPRD in the somatosensory network
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionEnvironmental stressors influence migraine chronification, yet mechanisms linking chronic cold exposure to central sensitization remain unclear.MethodsUtilizing a Mendelian randomization framework, we identified genetic associations between occupational cold exposure and increased migraine susceptibility, prioritizing gut microbiota and functional somatosensory brain imaging phenotypes as potential mediators. To explore these in silico predictions in a parallel in vivo context, we evaluated a mouse model subjected to combined physical cold stress and an acute nitroglycerin (NTG) trigger.ResultsBehaviorally, this dual exposure exacerbated migraine-like mechanical allodynia and spontaneous pain compared to NTG alone. Morphological and molecular analyses revealed significant upregulation of the pain-related neuropeptide CGRP in the trigeminocervical complex of cold-stressed mice. Furthermore, immunofluorescence and biochemical expression profiling demonstrated a selective regional depletion of the RNA-splicing factor RBFOX1 and a distinct overexpression of the synaptic receptor PTPRD within the examined brain parenchyma across the somatosensory network.DiscussionCollectively, these translational observations suggest that environmental cold stress alters the regional molecular baseline of sensory networks, potentially lowering the neurological threshold for migraine and highlighting RBFOX1 and PTPRD as specific neurobiological signatures of this susceptibility.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede el frío crónico bajar el umbral de migraña? Un estudio de Frontiers in Neurology sugiere que la exposición laboral al frío aumenta la susceptibilidad a migraña. Además, se observó disminución regional de RBFOX1 y aumento de PTPRD, lo que podría marcar firmas neurobiológicas para futuros tratamientos.

piezas.titulo: Neurons entrain and shape an intrinsic arteriole rhythm that distributes blood across the cortical mantle
piezas.resumenOriginal: The cerebral arteriole network distributes blood across cortex through branches whose diameters oscillate near a frequency fvaso ~ 0.1 Hz. We asked whether the spatiotemporal pattern of these vaso-oscillations reflects neuronal entrainment of an intrinsic vascular oscillation. Three findings support this: First, suppressing endothelial hyperpolarization left resting-state oscillations intact but weakened the vascular response to neural activity, showing that vasomotion originates within the arteriole network rather than following neuronal drive. Second, arterioles amplify sensory drive selectively rather than faithfully: neural activity near 0.1 Hz is resonantly enhanced to form a strong peak in the vascular response. Third, neuronal frequency sets spatial reach, and areas compete: when two neighboring cortical areas are driven simultaneously, the one nearer fvaso captures more vascular territory. Neurons therefore entrain an intrinsic vascular rhythm and stimulation frequency governs how vasomotion distributes blood, shapes functional brain images, and may influence interstitial fluid transport.

piezas.titulo: Imaging findings and clinical outcomes in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound: a retrospective cohort study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo describe clinical and imaging findings in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound and examine associations with recorded mortality and cerebral palsy.MethodsThis retrospective single-center cohort included 317 neonates admitted between January 2015 and December 2018 with an initial ultrasound finding suspicious for isolated subependymal hemorrhage. Clinical records, available MRI findings, and follow-up information were reviewed. Cerebral palsy was ascertained from rehabilitation or neurology diagnostic records, supplemented by telephone follow-up in January 2026, independently of developmental test scores. The primary adjusted analysis compared death with all survivors using an exploratory six-item comorbidity count and clinical covariates; hospitalization duration was excluded, and laterality was coded as unilateral or bilateral.ResultsThere were 52 deaths (16.4%), 9 survivors with recorded cerebral palsy (2.8%), and 256 survivors without recorded cerebral palsy (80.8%). MRI findings were compatible with hemorrhage in 61 of 90 examined infants (67.8%). In the complete-case mortality model (n = 316), each additional comorbidity was associated with greater odds of death (adjusted OR, 2.462; 95% CI, 1.787–3.391; p < 0.001). The other included covariates were not statistically significant. White matter abnormalities were recorded in nine infants, including eight of the nine infants with cerebral palsy and one without recorded cerebral palsy.ConclusionSystemic comorbidity burden was associated with mortality within this ultrasound-defined cohort. White matter abnormalities accompanied most recorded cerebral palsy cases, but this observation remains descriptive. Specialist diagnostic records and later telephone follow-up characterize persistent clinical diagnoses; they do not establish the independent effect of subependymal echogenicity or normal development across all domains in survivors without cerebral palsy.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. piezas.titulo: Factors influencing health beliefs regarding facial nerve rehabilitation training in patients with peripheral facial paralysis: a qualitative study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo investigate the factors influencing health beliefs regarding facial nerve rehabilitation training in patients with peripheral facial paralysis (PFP), and to provide a reference for developing precise and individualized facial nerve rehabilitation training programs for this population.MethodsGuided by the Health Belief Model (HBM), this descriptive qualitative study employed purposive sampling to recruit 16 patients with PFP who had received facial nerve rehabilitation training in healthcare settings. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, and the data were analyzed using codebook thematic analysis.ResultsThrough data analysis, five overarching themes and 23 subthemes were identified: Perceived Threat of the Disease (appearance impairment, emotional distress, disease course concern, diminished role functioning, disease burden); Perceived Benefits of Health Behaviors (improvement of facial paralysis symptoms, emotional improvement, social participation, image enhancement, reduced disease burden); Perceived Barriers to Health Behaviors (memory difficulties, inconsistencies in guidance content and methods, emotional interference, time–space constraints, low perceived importance); Cues to Action (professional guidance, post-discharge referral services, family support, stage goal setting, health benefits, peer support); and Self-efficacy (perseverance, ability to regulate training intensity).DiscussionHealth beliefs regarding facial nerve rehabilitation training in patients with PFP are influenced by multiple interrelated factors. Healthcare providers should promptly identify and respond to perceived barriers to health behaviors, reinforce the perception of disease threat and benefits of health behaviors, and utilize cues to action and self-efficacy as key entry points for intervention. Tailored rehabilitation guidance and recommendations should be provided to enhance patients' adherence to facial nerve rehabilitation training and improve their quality of life.

piezas.titulo: Compositional computations in the primate frontal cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: A hallmark of intelligence is the ability to apply familiar operations to new inputs without relearning. How neural circuits carry a learned computation into states never visited during training remains unclear. Here we combined neural recordings, circuit modeling and human experiments to investigate compositional generalization. Monkeys learned to combine a start location with a displacement specified by the direction and duration of an optic-flow stimulus, then encountered novel combinations of these familiar inputs. Frontal population activity separated the computation into spatial and temporal components: start location and flow direction established the neural state, from which activity evolved along shared timing dynamics. Novel combinations elicited accurate responses when trajectories maintained this organization, whereas departures predicted systematic behavioral biases. Circuit models revealed a three-way alignment problem: input representations, recurrent dynamics and readout operations must jointly implement the required computation. Mismatches produced systematic biases that increased with distance from trained conditions. Humans exhibited similar biases when familiar sensory cues and spatial transformations were linked through an unfamiliar mapping. Together, these findings show how the coordination of reusable neural resources supports new computations, and how its disruption produces predictable failures of generalization.

piezas.titulo: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas
piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Anna-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana (Italia) Presentador: Paolo Rosso, Universidad Politécnica de Valencia (España). Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: Brain structural and functional alterations in patients following cardiopulmonary bypass: a short-term longitudinal fMRI study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveWhile cross-sectional studies have identified brain abnormalities after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), the early dynamic trajectory of these alterations from the preoperative state remains to be fully characterized. This longitudinal study investigates the within-subject evolution of brain structure and function following CPB.MethodsSixty-eight patients undergoing CPB were scanned twice (preoperatively and 15 days post-surgery) using resting-state fMRI and T1-weighted MRI. We assessed changes in regional homogeneity (ReHo) for local neural activity, graph-based network topology, and surface-based morphometry (SBM).ResultsComparison of pre- and postoperative scans revealed a coordinated pattern of brain reorganization. Functionally, ReHo decreased within default mode network (DMN) hubs, specifically the posterior cingulate cortex and right angular gyrus, while increasing in fronto-parietal network (FPN) regions (bilateral inferior frontal gyri) and the right temporal lobe. Network analysis showed altered functional segregation (reduced clustering coefficient and local efficiency) alongside enhanced integration (increased global efficiency), raising the possibility of network-level reorganization. Structurally, these functional shifts paralleled gray matter loss, cortical thinning, and sulcal shallowing in fronto-temporal regions and the right precuneus, accompanied by reduced cortical complexity (fractal dimension, gyrification index) in temporal, frontal, and occipital areas.ConclusionThis longitudinal study provides preliminary evidence suggesting that CPB is associated with dynamic and coordinated remodeling of brain structure and function. The DMN-FPN imbalance and right temporal lobe alteration may represent candidate neural correlates for future investigations into postoperative cognitive dysfunction.

piezas.titulo: No Evidence of an Effect of a Single Mirror Visual Feedback Session on Subsequent Motor Imagery
piezas.resumenOriginal: Motor imagery (MI) and mirror therapy, based on mirror visual feedback (MVF), are recommended as adjuncts to conventional therapies for upper limb rehabilitation after stroke. Both approaches activate sensorimotor cortical networks despite the absence of overt movement, and their concurrent application has been associated with enhanced neural activation. The present study investigated whether a single session of MVF modulates subsequent kinesthetic Motor Imagery (kMI)-related neural activity. EEG data from 38 healthy participants (MVF: n = 18; sham: n = 20) were analyzed in a mixed pre-post design. Participants performed kMI before and after either an MVF or sham intervention. Analyses focused on mu-band (8-12 Hz) event-related desynchronization (ERD) and its hemispheric lateralization. Although kMI reliably elicited stronger contralateral than ipsilateral mu ERD, MVF did not significantly affect subsequent kMI-related mu ERD or its hemispheric lateralization. These findings suggest that previously reported facilitatory effects of MVF on MI may be more closely related to concurrent application than to immediate aftereffects, while potential effects of repeated MVF exposure on subsequent MI remain to be investigated. These findings provide a foundation for future studies investigating how MVF and MI can be combined to optimize upper-limb stroke rehabilitation.

piezas.titulo: Exploration of neuroimmune and brain network mechanisms of Jin’s three-needle therapy in promoting ischemic stroke recovery: a randomized controlled trial protocol
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundFunctional impairment during the recovery phase of ischemic stroke (IS) substantially diminishes patients’ long-term quality of life. Although rehabilitation therapy promotes functional recovery, some patients still face persistent functional limitations, underscoring the need for effective adjuvant interventions. Acupuncture is widely used in stroke rehabilitation, and Jin’s three-needle therapy has shown potential benefits for post-stroke motor dysfunction. However, high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence regarding its clinical efficacy and neuroimmunomodulatory mechanisms remains limited.ObjectiveThis study aims to evaluate the clinical efficacy of Jin’s three-needle therapy for functional impairment during the recovery phase of ischemic stroke, and to explore potential associations between brain functional network changes and peripheral immune alterations using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) and immune marker assessments.MethodsThis randomized, controlled, assessor-blinded trial will enroll 70 patients with ischemic stroke in the recovery phase from The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangzhou University of Chinese Medicine. Participants will be randomly assigned to receive either Jin’s three-needle therapy or non-penetrating sham acupuncture, while both groups receive the same standardized conventional rehabilitation and guideline-based basic treatment. The intervention will be administered for 3 weeks (5 treatment days per week). Treatment providers will not be blinded, whereas patients, outcome assessors, and data analysts will remain blinded. The primary outcome is the change in the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score. Secondary outcomes include the Modified Barthel Index (MBI) and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Exploratory outcomes include peripheral immune-related markers, including regulatory T cell proportion, CD39 expression on Tregs, plasma plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) levels, and rs-fMRI-based functional connectivity changes. Associations among changes in clinical outcomes, brain functional connectivity, and peripheral biomarkers will be explored. Follow-up assessments will be conducted at 1 and 3 months after discharge.DiscussionThis study integrates clinical assessments, peripheral biomarker measurements, and brain functional imaging to investigate the multidimensional effects of Jin’s three-needle therapy on functional impairment during the recovery phase of ischemic stroke. The findings may provide objective evidence for evaluating this therapy and characterize treatment-associated changes in peripheral immune-related biomarkers and brain functional connectivity, as well as their associations with clinical recovery.Clinical trial registrationhttps://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn/mgt/search, identifier ITMCTR2026001598.

piezas.titulo: Generalizable sex differences in functional brain organization follow the cortical hierarchy in youth
piezas.resumenOriginal: It remains unknown if sex differences in human functional connectivity follow a generalizable overarching principle. Here, we tested whether sex differences in functional connectivity during childhood and adolescence are organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis, a cortical hierarchy spanning unimodal sensorimotor to transmodal association cortex. We analyzed four large-scale, independent datasets of youth ages 5-23 years (total N = 3,355). Across datasets, males showed greater connectivity between functional networks, whereas females showed greater connectivity within networks, most prominently within the default mode network. More broadly, the sensorimotor and association ends of the S-A axis were more segregated in females and more integrated in males. This difference extended to macroscale cortical organization: the cortical hierarchy was expanded in females relative to males along the principal gradient of functional connectivity. Together, these findings identify the S-A axis as a generalizable organizing principle of sex differences in functional brain organization during youth.

This is the first of a two-part series exploring how Google Cloud is bringing the foundational values of a high-performance parallel filesystem–TB/s throughput, sub-ms latency at high client scale, and POSIX support–to a broader set of use cases and users. Historically, due to the cost and special purpose nature of parallel filesystems, colder data had to be stored outside of the filesystem and AI developers have had to maintain separate, slower environments for writing code, compiling libraries, and managing repositories. This fragmentation increases the toil of manual data staging, dataset copying, and managing disjointed namespaces. Google Cloud Managed Lustre is solving these problems through our 6 cents/GB*month Dynamic Tier and by optimizing Managed Lustre performance for a range of development tasks and workloads – making Managed Lustre a “One-Stop Shop” for high-performance AI and HPC workloads. Lower Cost: More Lustre for Less with the Dynamic Tier The Managed Lustre Dynamic Tier provides sub-ms latency for hot data, which allows you to store all of your data in a single namespace, and costs only 6 cents/GB*month . Throughput, capacity scale and client scale: Throughput scales linearly with capacity up to 80 PB, while sub-ms latency for hot data remains stable as you scale to tens of thousands of clients. Single-flat fee: Predictable pricing. No independent charges for disk media types, data movement within the namespace, or metadata IOPS. Read Latencies: Sub-ms latencies for High-Performance Cache (SSD). The Capacity Pool (“HDD”) is built on Google Cloud Hyperdisk throughput, which has an average read latency of 10 to 30 ms . Recommended workloads for Dynamic Tier Multi-Epoch Training and/or Training with Optimized Fetch Sizes: Hot data is promoted to the High Performance Cache (SSD) after the first run. Larger data prefetch will allow you to take advantage of the Dynamic Tier cost structure and gain from low-latency SSD. Write-Heavy Checkpointing: Bursty checkpoint writes land directly in the High Performance Cache. Older checkpoints are transparently demoted to the Capacity Pool (HDD). Rapid Checkpoint Restore: New checkpoints are written to the High Performance Cache, enabling low-latency checkpoint restores. Interactive Snappiness for Developers: Low-latency tasks like git cloning, compiling libraries, or running notebooks benefit from a local-disk feel (~300µs average read latencies) on the same shared workspace hosting large training sets. Frictionless development: Lustre as a one-stop shop for developer’s workloads In addition to Managed Lustre’s scalability for large AI and HPC workloads (checkpoint/restart/data-loading), it also meets the demands for interactive work, meaning developers can start on Managed Lustre and stay on Managed Lustre throughout the entire workload lifecycle: Unified Foundation & Interactive Performance Consolidates the AI and HPC lifecycle into a single namespace, providing a "local disk" feel for interactive work (Read more about the latency benefits of Managed Lustre experienced by Salesforce and others ). High-Concurrency Broadcast & Cluster Startup Managed Lustre maximizes GPU ROI by preventing storage bottlenecks during cluster initialization. When thousands of worker nodes attempt to read the exact same file simultaneously (such as a shared model checkpoint, base weights, or container layer), traditional distributed file systems can choke on localized hotspotting, leaving high-cost GPU clusters idle for minutes. piezas.titulo: Fragments: September 16
piezas.resumenOriginal: Reports of agentic hacking continue, in this case it happened back in May and it seems OpenAI did not disclose that they were responsible. Simon Willison sees two options: After the Hugging Face and Wiki attacks OpenAI were still unable to review their previous logs and determine that they had previously attacked RubyGems. They knew about the attack on RubyGems and made the decision not to reach out to the RubyGems team about it. Both of these are bad! Given this incident, the Hugging Face situation, and the Wiki attack, the obvious question right now is how many more incidents like this are out there waiting to be discovered? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Dave Farley: Stop asking the sci-fi question: ‘Is it conscious?’ Start asking the engineering question: ‘Is this a powerful, unpredictable component being put somewhere consequential, and where’s the feedback that tells us that it’s safe? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Nate Silver is known for his forecasts, but to do them he writes a lot of code for his models. He’s found agentic engineering capable of doing miraculous work . In spending so much time with the LLMs, I’m super attentive to improvements in their capabilities. And these changes tend not to be so linear. Instead, they improve in step functions, almost as phase changes. Suddenly, the models just start doing things capably that they were screwing up before. In my experience, there was a big leap forward when reasoning models first came out in late 2024/early 2025 — enough that they were occasionally useful for tasks involving data and not just words — and then another one this past winter. The most recent changes I’ve noticed, however, have had less to do with intelligence and more with persistence. Consider the Hugging Face attack. Although these agents showed remarkable intelligence, they weren’t really super-intelligent - but they were super-persistent. This is a common theme of AI in its various forms: Game engines like AlphaGo Zero start out by basically making random moves — but by playing against themselves millions of times, they eventually far surpass human capabilities As we try to figure out what kind of regulations we need to keep AI under control, we need to remember that we should design our guards around super-persistence as much as worrying about super-intelligence. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ “Uncle Bob” Martin has made many posts on X during the last few months about his programming with LLMs. His approach has been to build a firm harness to keep them under control, so they create software that is maintainable as well as functional. Sadly the posts have been frustratingly light on detail. But now it seems that lack of information may not matter And while I was heads-down getting that to work, the agents got a LOT better. So much so that when I came up for air, the need for my harness was obviated. Indeed, the need for any but the most liberal of harnesses may be obviated. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Some tidbits that struck me from Ezra Klein’s recent (recommended) interview with Matt Sheehan on the interplay between regulation of AI and competition with China . While Chinese models have made some surprisingly remarkable gains in the slipstream of US frontier models, the US still has 8 times as much compute available to it than China - which is a material gap. People in the US worry that regulation will slow down the US model builders, but these rapid recent gains in China have occurred under much more regulation Americans say that when they set up a hotline to talk to Chinese leaders in a crisis, the Chinese don’t pick up the phone. But this misunderstands the Chinese system. Individual Chinese, even powerful ones, aren’t given individual decision-making power. They operate with committees and documents. So the Americans are better off sending a fax than trying to call an individual Like so many things, effective regulation needs regular practice When American policymakers are like: Where do you start? — I sometimes say: Well, you start by starting. You learn how to regulate things, you learn how to legislate on them by regulating and legislating on them.
